Swiss Federal Supreme Court decision of June 22, 1988 (BGE 114 II 264) (translated with 
Deepl) 
6 of 10 
Based on the established breaches of contract, the defendant owes a contractual penalty. The 
lower court reduced the amount of this penalty from the agreed amount to CHF 10,000. The 
breach of the non-competition clause was deemed very minor. Furthermore, the plaintiff did not 
suffer any damage and failed to demonstrate any risk of damage. She merely asserted that the 
candidates were confused by the letter, offering a single email from one candidate as evidence. 
However, nothing in that email supports her case. The plaintiff should have explained why the 
candidate’s confusion was attributable to the expert’s letter. It failed to do so. The same applies to 
the plaintiff’s claim that the statements in breach of contract, such as “leading headhunter,” had 
or could have had a negative impact on its business. 
Nor did she explain how many experts were in the database, how many of them were involved in 
(ongoing) placement processes on January 11, 2021, and whether experts who were not involved 
in ongoing processes had ceased to use the plaintiff’s services in response to the expert’s letter. 
While it is not her responsibility to prove her damages in numerical terms, she nevertheless 
should have substantively contested the defendant’s assertion that the experts’ letter had no 
negative consequences for her and should have demonstrated, at least in broad terms, the 
existence of damage or a risk of damage. The plaintiff failed to meet this obligation. Therefore, a 
substantial reduction of the contractual penalty is warranted. Furthermore, the fact that a 
recurrence of the breach is practically impossible works in the defendant’s favor. By contrast, the 
legal transaction underlying the non-competition clause was financially significant, which in 
principle justifies higher contractual penalties. A complete waiver is therefore not justified, 
especially since the contractual penalty always serves a punitive function as well. Moreover, 
even the defendant did not request a reduction to zero. All things considered, a contractual 
penalty in the very low five-digit range or CHF 10,000 is appropriate.  
4.3. The considerations summarized above are convincing. Neither the plaintiff nor the defendant 
argues in their respective appeals that the lower court determined the facts arbitrarily or violated 
federal law.  
4.3.1. The defendant continues to deny a violation of the non-competition clause. He reiterates 
that it was permissible to refer in the expert’s letter to an actual takeover of Construction21 by 
Arkadium. Arkadium had taken over not only all employees and ongoing placement processes,
